paragraphs.heading: Logic is careful reasoning
paragraphs.edited: When you think of logic, who comes to mind? Probably somebody like Sherlock Holmes, who uses his wit and mind to outsmart his opponents. Maybe you feel this way when you've had a conversation with somebody with a different belief system, or when you're sharing your faith. It's as if it's this jockeying back and forth, trying to outsmart each other with logic. This can certainly happen, but technically logic is just a careful and proper use of reason. Logic is important for Christians so we can arrive at truthful beliefs ourselves, but it's also important in conversations with other people so we can help them arrive at truth in a loving manner. Let me share a story that might help.

paragraphs.heading: A conversation with a professor
paragraphs.edited: Some time ago, when I was a graduate student studying philosophy, I had a memorable conversation with a professor from an Ivy League school. He said to me, oh, I think it's great that you're studying philosophy as a Christian. Maybe you'd want to study Buddhist philosophy, because all religions are true. Now, that struck me as very odd. I thought for a minute, wait a minute, how could all religions be true when they contradict on such fundamental teachings about God, the afterlife, and how you get salvation? So I simply asked him a question. I said, do you mind if I ask you a question? How could all religions be true, namely Islam and Christianity?

paragraphs.edited: Muslims say if you believe Jesus is God, you've committed the sin of shirk, and you're certainly going to hell. I said, Christians say you can't get to heaven unless you believe Jesus is God. How can both of these be true? He kind of fumbled around a little bit. We kept talking. Eventually he looked at me and said, here's the deal. He said, religion aside, what really is true is cultural relativism. Therefore, you should be tolerant.

paragraphs.heading: Spotting the inconsistency
paragraphs.edited: Now stop and think about this. Use your mind, your logic, to analyze this claim. He said he believed in cultural relativism, which says morality and truth depend upon the culture. But then he turned to me and said, therefore, because morality is relative, I should be tolerant. Now do you see the inconsistency? If morality is relative, he can't turn to me and say I ought to be tolerant, because he's appealing to tolerance as if it's a universal truth claim that everybody should follow. On the flip side, if he says that everybody should be tolerant, then he doesn't actually believe that morality is relative, because he's appealing to the universal principle or standard of tolerance.

paragraphs.edited: Friends, people hold a lot of different views about God, religion, and morality, and one important thing to do is to listen to their views and draw them out. What we'll often see, when we do that, is that their views will lead to inconsistency and sometimes even to logical absurdity.

paragraphs.heading: Reducing a view to absurdity
paragraphs.edited: For example, in Matthew 22:41 through 45, Jesus uses the known logical principle of reductio ad absurdum. Now, that sounds really fancy, but essentially what it means is reducing a position to absurdity. In this passage in Matthew, Jesus is having a conversation with the Pharisees, and he asks them, who do you think the Messiah is? Is the Messiah the son of David? And they say yes, the Messiah is the son of David. What Jesus says is meant to draw out their view to show that it leads to absurdity. Now, how does he do this?

And they say yes, the Messiah is the son of David. And what Jesus says is meant to draw out their view to show that it leads to absurdity. Now, how does he do this?

paragraphs.edited: He quotes from Psalms 110:1, in which David, who wrote that psalm, says that the Messiah is his Lord. And Jesus says, wait a minute, you just said that the Messiah is the son of David, but now we have David calling the Messiah Lord. How can that be? Now, what is Jesus' point? He's saying, if you think that the Messiah is merely the son of David, then that leads to absurdity. Rather, it's more reasonable to conclude that yes, the Messiah is the son of David, but he's more than human. He actually is Lord, as David himself said in Psalms 110 verse 1.

paragraphs.heading: Grow up in your thinking
paragraphs.edited: In my conversation with an Ivy League professor, I was trying to show that he held two views in contradiction that, when drawn to their logical conclusion, led to absurdity. This is exactly what Jesus was doing with the Pharisees. This is why the Apostle Paul, in Ephesians 4 verses 14 through 15, says we are not to be like children in terms of our thinking, tossed to and fro by different waves of doctrine. Rather, we are to grow up and be mature in the way we think.

paragraphs.heading: Speak truth in love
paragraphs.edited: Paul also says in this passage that we are to speak truth in love. In other words, we are called to speak truth. We can't compromise truth. We don't speak truth just to win arguments. We don't speak truth just to prove people wrong. We do it because we know that it's only truth that can set people free.

paragraphs.heading: A lifelong process
paragraphs.edited: And please keep in mind, your conversations will not always go as smoothly as they seem to go with me and the Ivy League professor. In fact, more often than not, after a conversation I have with somebody, I'll step away and go, oh, I should have said this. Oh, next time, I'll say that. Learning to love God with our minds and use logic is a lifelong process. You're learning some powerful stuff about truth and defending the faith in this entire study that we're going through.

paragraphs.heading: Not to win arguments
paragraphs.edited: It's easy to start thinking, great, I'm going to write this down, I'm going to go online, I'm going to go in person to my parents, my friends, other nonbelievers, and win some arguments. If that's what you're thinking, you're missing the point. The point of this is not to go out and win arguments. The point of this is, number one, to know truth for ourselves, and then second, to be able to speak that truth in love, to use reason, to use logic, to love people. That way, as people draw closer to you and learn more about your faith, they find something genuine and real that is not easily put out.
